english-web-hq.why: Filtered English web is where the model learns to reason at all, and the capability an India-first model is least likely to be judged on. It gave up five points to the skills tiers on the argument that code teaches reasoning too — which is a bet, and the tier to watch if general reasoning regresses.

code.why: Code is a primary capability, not a garnish, and it transfers: models trained on more code reason better in prose. The permissive subset only, because the licence position on the rest is unresolved.

math-stem.why: Reasoning-dense text buys more per token than anything else in the mix. Almost none of it exists in Indian languages, which is itself one of the findings.

indic-natural.why: The only tier carrying what the languages actually know. It is also the scarcest, which is why it is read four times and why it sits in the protected lane — an English-biased quality filter scores it as noise and drops it.

indic-synthetic.why: Manufactured text fills the volume the natural pool cannot reach. It buys fluency and reasoning transfer; it does not buy culture, and counting it as natural Indic is the commonest way to overstate a corpus.

india-context-english.why: English text about India. It teaches the worldview without paying the tokenizer tax — and it is the capability the benchmark set can least reliably detect.

agentic-traces.why: Multi-step tool use has to be trained on, not prompted into existence. Traces are scarce and filtered hard, so they share the protected lane.

indic-knowledge-systems.sources: Ayurveda and Siddha · Jyotish and Panchang · NDLI and DLI scans
indic-knowledge-systems.why: Indian knowledge systems, and the one tier no frontier model has any reason to build. Most of it exists only as scanned pages in institutional archives, so it is an OCR problem before it is a data problem — which is exactly why nobody else has it and why it is worth the collection cost.

indic-civilizational.sources: Vedic corpus · classical Sanskrit · Upanishads · Dharmashastra
indic-civilizational.why: The civilizational literature an India-first model is expected to reason from rather than merely quote. It is small, largely public-domain, and mostly digitised badly. Reading it twice costs almost nothing; not having it at all is the difference between a model that knows India and one that has read about it.

general-web.why: Breadth — everyday knowledge and common sense, and the least interesting tier per token. It used to be the largest here, and gave up seven points to code, maths and tool use, because the assignment names those as primary capabilities and a mixture is zero-sum.

priors.claim: Up to 4 epochs of repeated data is almost as good as fresh data: an 8.7B-parameter model trained for 4 epochs on 44B unique tokens finished with only 0.5% higher validation loss than a single-epoch model on 178B unique tokens. The fitted decay constant R*_D is 15.4, which the paper rounds to 15 when it names the half-life — a repeated token has lost 1/e of its value at around 15 repetitions (16 epochs) — and no amount of repetition beats a single epoch on U·(1 + R*_D) ~= 16x the unique pool.
priors.source: arXiv:2305.16264 — Muennighoff et al., Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models
priors.effect_on_design: Re-budgets the corpus as unique pool x deliberate epoch schedule = effective tokens instead of '15T unique tokens'. The ~0.3T unique natural Indic pool at 4 epochs is ~1.2T effective at near-zero quality cost, raising the natural-Indic effective share from 2% to ~7-8% without collecting a single new token (theoretical ceiling ~4.8T effective at 16x). Also half-defuses the 40-70% global-dedup loss risk: dedup down to the unique pool, then choose repetition deliberately.

priors.claim: At 40 epochs, repeating data is worthless, and some 44-epoch runs diverge mid-training.
priors.source: arXiv:2305.16264 — Muennighoff et al., Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models
priors.effect_on_design: Sets a hard upper bound on any epoch schedule: repetition budgets must stay far below 40 epochs, and divergence — not just diminishing returns — is the failure mode past that point.

priors.claim: Allocation rule under data constraint: scale epochs faster than parameters, because excess parameters decay in value faster than repeated data (R*_N < R*_D). This is the opposite of what naively extending Chinchilla predicts.
priors.source: arXiv:2305.16264 — Muennighoff et al., Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models
priors.effect_on_design: When the Indic pool is fixed, spend the marginal FLOP on more epochs over the scarce high-value tiers rather than on more parameters. Directly contradicts the Chinchilla-style arithmetic the main report's Section 16 used.

priors.claim: Mixing code data into a data-constrained run 'gives the ability to scale an additional 2x'.
priors.source: arXiv:2305.16264 — Muennighoff et al., Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models
priors.effect_on_design: The code tier is not just a capability tier — it buys headroom against the data ceiling, which reinforces keeping Stack v2 permissive + Nemotron code at a meaningful share of the mix.

priors.claim: Up-sampling just 0.1% of the corpus 100x significantly degrades performance. Repetition works on whole tiers, not on tiny slivers hammered repeatedly.
priors.source: Hernandez et al., cited within arXiv:2305.16264
priors.effect_on_design: Constrains how the epoch schedule may be applied: repeat the whole natural-Indic or curated-clean tier, never a small favoured subset. Rules out 'just loop the 64B Sangraha-verified slice' as a shortcut.

priors.claim: Once expected inference demand is accounted for, the compute optimum shifts toward smaller models trained on more tokens than Chinchilla prescribes.
priors.effect_on_design: Formal justification for training well past compute-optimal, and — at India-population deployment scale — pressure toward maximising active-parameter efficiency (MoE with a small active count) rather than total parameters.

priors.claim: Running the OPUS per-iteration data selector at the 5B stage cost a ~17% wall-clock tax: 30,429 tok/s with OPUS active vs 36,737 tok/s ordinary — despite amortizing each scoring pass over 10 training steps and implementing Ghost extraction, CountSketch projection (m=8192) and the per-step preconditioner as custom kernels. The originating OPUS paper reports 4.7% end-to-end overhead, but in synchronous data-parallel training without ZeRO-style sharding; integration with sharded parameters is where 4.7% became ~17%.
priors.effect_on_design: Prices dynamic data selection honestly for a 300B run. Budget the selector's cost against a sharded stack, not against the paper's headline overhead. OPUS defaults recorded: buffer b=64, temperature tau=0.9, sketch m=8192.

priors.claim: OPUS was active at the 5B stage only — disabled at 2B (easy-token regime; candidates differed too little in utility to be worth scoring) and disabled again from 9B onward. The 8x compute-reduction result that motivates OPUS (GPT-2 XL / FineWeb) did not transfer cheaply into the production stack.
priors.effect_on_design: Demotes dynamic selection to ablation-stage tooling rather than the production backbone at 300B, and confirms the static, phase-scheduled mixture as the backbone — that is what the only in-project 120B run actually shipped with.

priors.claim: The Golden Proxy that OPUS steers toward is English-heavy (cosine 0.876 with the English web band), so the selector systematically under-values Indic data and would reject it if allowed to govern everything. LightningLM therefore reserves an Always-ON tier of 78.1B tokens — 8% of every batch, invisible to the selector — protecting Indic data and benchmark training splits. Stated principle: 'A single selector should not govern data whose value it cannot see.'
priors.effect_on_design: Add an Always-ON lane of ~8% of every batch reserved for Tier-2/Tier-3 Indic scripts plus agentic/world-model traces and benchmark training splits, bypassing every selector and quality classifier. FineWeb-Edu-style quality classifiers carry the same English-proxy bias, so the lane is the mechanism that guarantees Bodo, Santali, Dogri and Manipuri actually train at every stage.

priors.claim: Contamination discipline has an existence proof at 120B scale: LightningLM dropped pool B2 (31.3B tokens — a full pool) for contamination, and kept the 6.8M-token Golden Proxy (11 shards) strictly held out, never trained on.
priors.effect_on_design: Validates the mandatory train/validate/test quarantine of Section 12.3 as operationally survivable — dropping a whole pool is an acceptable cost, and the steering proxy must never enter the training mix.

priors.claim: A 120B sparse MoE (460 routed experts, top-12 routing, 5.93B active ~= 5% of 118.67B stored) was grown in four stages from a 1.78B dense seed (1.78B -> 5B -> 9B -> 120B), trained end-to-end on a single eight-GPU node, early stages at 4K context and 9B+ at 8K, at roughly 67 days and ~$100K-class without spot pricing.
priors.effect_on_design: Shifts the burden of proof onto training a 300B from scratch. Combined with Sarvam-105B being Apache 2.0 with its full MoE recipe published, the capital question becomes 'scratch vs grow'; the document inserts a 4-week head-to-head at ~2B scale (from-scratch vs grown/upcycled on identical data, judged on Indic + code held-out loss) before any capital commitment.

priors.claim: Measured on FLORES-200 across six tokenizers and fourteen Indian languages: under cl100k_base (GPT-3.5/GPT-4) Indian languages pay an average 8.0x tokenization tax vs English, reaching 13.0x for Malayalam, reducing the effective context window to as little as 12% of what English users get for equivalent semantic content. The mechanism is failed byte-pair merges leaving text fragmented into single-byte tokens (merge failure correlates with tax at Pearson r = 0.89). XLM-R and o200k_base reduce the average Indic tax by 73% — this is a tokenizer design failure, not a property of Indic scripts.
priors.effect_on_design: Elevates the tokenizer from a workstream to a gating milestone: nothing else starts until fertility is validated across all 22 scripts. Also argues that the o200k retrofit path starts materially closer to the goal than the main report assumed.

priors.claim: Indic scripts are punished by English-centric BPE at 4-8 tokens per word. Sarvam reports achieving fertility of 1.4-2.1 across Indian languages, which they translate into a 200-400% efficiency gain. Stated conclusion: 'Your tokenizer decision is worth more than 2T extra tokens.'
priors.source: Sarvam (reported in Atlas Section 1.3); target restated in Section 17 and Section 18.1
priors.effect_on_design: Fixes the fertility target for the project's own tokenizer at 1.4-2.1 across all 22 scripts, including Ol Chiki and Meitei Mayek, tested before the tokenizer is frozen; it is also the pipeline's stated mixing/tokenization acceptance criterion.

priors.claim: Morphology-aware SentencePiece BPE tokenizers trained on a 781MB balanced corpus across seven languages, handling Sanskrit/Tamil agglutination and sandhi, achieve 2.6 tokens per Indian Knowledge System technical term vs 5.25 for GPT-2, and ~90% sequence-length reduction vs GPT-2/byte-level on a released 490-sentence IKS test set (measurement script published).
priors.effect_on_design: Supplies a published, reproducible measurement harness for the fertility gate and evidence that morphology-aware segmentation is where the Indic compression gains come from.

priors.claim: BrahmicTokenizer-131K is a byte-level BPE that retrofits o200k_base via a two-stage procedure (script-prune crop plus surgical installation of Brahmic vocabulary), closing the Indic compression gap at the 131K-vocab class while preserving English and code compression. It deliberately declines language-aware pre-tokenization to stay drop-in compatible. It is the tokenizer used across the entire LightningLM family.
priors.effect_on_design: Candidate recipe 1 for the 300B tokenizer: retrofit preserves the English/code frontier and ecosystem compatibility, and is the demonstrated-in-production choice.

priors.claim: Kronecker embeddings replace the ~537M-parameter embedding table at that vocabulary/width with a 33.55M-parameter projection — negligible at 120B, but most of a quarter of the model at the 1.78B seed.
priors.effect_on_design: Makes a large Indic-capable vocabulary affordable at the small end of a staged-growth plan, which is what allows growth to start from a 1.78B dense seed rather than a wider one.

priors.claim: MUTANT-Indic is a 200K shared-vocabulary SuperBPE-based tokenizer trained on a 10GB sample drawn from ~50GB of curated multilingual data (OLMo, Wikipedia, books, PDFs, Common Crawl, Sangraha; code from Stack v2), via fastText LID -> MinHash dedup -> NFKC normalization -> script validation, FineWeb-style.
priors.effect_on_design: Candidate recipe 2 for the 300B tokenizer: from-scratch at 200K (the Sarvam path, fertility 1.4-2.1) maximises Indic fertility at the cost of re-deriving English/code performance. The gate is unchanged either way — fertility validated on all 22 scripts before any other workstream commits.
